type: classifying — picks out the most important one of a group
position: attributive only — never after a verb: *the main problem is cost*, not *the problem is main*
contrast: Russian *главный* can stand after a verb; *main* cannot. *Что здесь главное?* is *What matters most here?* and *Кто здесь главный?* is *Who's in charge here?*, never *Who is main here?* After a verb, use *the main one* or *most important*: *Price is the main thing*. The noun *main* is a large pipe or cable (*a water main burst*), and the adverb is *mainly* (*mainly on weekends*). The old sense 'full, all one's' survives only in the literary *by main force*.

senses.gloss: Largest, most important or most central of its kind.
examples: The *main* reason I moved here was the job.
The *main* entrance is on the other side of the building.
Do you want chicken or fish for the *main* course?

position: attributive only — never after a verb: *the chief problem*, not *the problem is chief*; the one exception is the fronted phrase *chief among*: *Chief among our worries was money*
contrast: The noun *chief* is the head of a group: *the police chief*, *the fire chief*. Do not confuse it with *chef* (шеф-повар). Russian *шеф* in the sense 'boss' is *boss* in everyday American English: *My boss is on vacation*; *my chief* sounds military or old-fashioned. After a verb the adjective does not work: say *Cost is the chief concern*, not *The concern is chief*. The adverb is *chiefly* (*chiefly in the summer*).

senses.gloss: Most important; main.
examples: The *chief* problem with the plan is that nobody can afford it.
Safety is our *chief* concern on the job site.
The *chief* complaint from customers is the long wait on the phone.

senses.gloss: Highest in rank or authority; at the head of a team or organization.
examples: She was promoted to *chief* engineer last spring.
The *chief* executive officer announced the layoffs in an email.
The *chief* financial officer will present the budget on Friday.

position: attributive only — never after a verb: *the principal cause*, not *the cause was principal*
contrast: *Principal* and *principle* sound exactly the same. *Principal* is the adjective 'main', and also a noun: the head of a school (директор школы) or the money you borrowed, not counting interest. *Principle* is only a noun, 'a basic rule or belief' (принцип): *a matter of principle*, *the principles of physics*. *Principal* is more formal than *main*; in conversation *the main reason* is more natural than *the principal reason*. The adverb is *principally*.

senses.gloss: Most important; main.
examples: Tourism is the *principal* source of income for the island.
The *principal* cause of the fire was faulty wiring.
Denver and Colorado Springs are the state's two *principal* cities.

senses.gloss: First in rank among a group of performers or researchers; leading.
examples: She was a *principal* dancer with the New York City Ballet for ten years.
He is the *principal* investigator on a federal research grant.
The *principal* cellist played the solo beautifully.

position: attributive only — right before the noun, after *a*, *the* or a possessive if there is one: *a mere child*, *mere seconds*; never *the child was mere*
comparison: not gradable — there is no *merer*, but the superlative *merest* adds extra emphasis: *the merest hint*
contrast: *Mere* stresses how small or unimportant something is. A singular noun or an amount takes *a* or *the* before it: *a mere $5*, *the mere fact*, not *mere $5*; a plural can stand alone: *mere minutes later*. After a verb use *only* or *just*: *The difference is only $5*, not *The difference is mere*. The adverb is *merely* (*I was merely asking*). *The mere* + noun says that this alone is enough: *the mere mention of his name* = одно только упоминание его имени.

senses.gloss: Nothing more than; only, used to stress that something is small or unimportant.
examples: She was a *mere* child when her family moved to Texas.
The tickets cost a *mere* $12, so the show sold out in hours.
The fire spread through the building in *mere* minutes.

senses.gloss: Even by itself, without anything more, used to say that something small has a big effect.
examples: The *mere* thought of flying makes him nervous.
The *merest* hint of criticism upsets her for days.
The *mere* fact that he called shows he's sorry.

position: both — attributive only in the main sense 'nothing but' (*sheer luck*); the senses 'very steep' and 'very thin' also follow a verb (*the drop is sheer*, *the curtains are sheer*)
comparison: not gradable — in the main sense 'nothing but'; but the 'thin' sense grades: *very sheer*, *sheerer*, *sheerest*
contrast: In its main sense *sheer* goes only before a noun and adds force: *sheer luck* = чистое везение, *the sheer size* = один только размер. *The luck was sheer* is not English. Do not confuse it with *shear* (same sound), a verb meaning 'to cut' (*shear sheep*); *shears* are large scissors. The verb *sheer* (*sheer off*, 'to swerve') and the noun *sheers* (thin curtains) are separate words.

senses.gloss: Nothing but; complete and total, used to stress how great something is.
examples: We found the place by *sheer* luck.
The *sheer* size of the Grand Canyon is hard to take in.
She finished the marathon through *sheer* willpower.

senses.gloss: Extremely steep; almost vertical.
examples: The trail runs along a *sheer* cliff with no railing.
On the north side, the drop to the river is *sheer*.

senses.gloss: Very thin and light, so that you can see through it.
examples: She wore a *sheer* black blouse over a camisole.
The curtains are *sheer*, so the room gets plenty of light.
For summer she wanted something *sheerer* than her winter tights.

position: attributive only — never after a verb: *an utter disaster*, not *the disaster was utter*
contrast: *Utter* goes mostly with bad or extreme nouns: *utter nonsense*, *utter chaos*, *utter silence*, *an utter failure*. For good things, *a complete success* or *a total success* is what people say. After a verb use *complete* or *total*: *The chaos was complete*. The verb *utter* is a different word, 'to say' (*She didn't utter a word* = не произнесла ни слова), and the adverb is *utterly* (*utterly exhausted*).

senses.gloss: Complete and total, used mostly to stress something bad or extreme.
examples: The first day of the move was an *utter* disaster.
That's *utter* nonsense, and you know it.
When the power went out, the house fell into *utter* darkness.

position: attributive only — never after a verb: *a former teacher*, not *the teacher is former*
form: an old comparative meaning 'earlier'; the adverb is *formerly*
contrast: Russian *бывший* also works alone as a noun (*мой бывший*); English uses *ex*: *my ex*, *my ex-husband*, not *my former*. *The former* standing alone is a pronoun-like noun, paired with *the latter*: *Of tea and coffee, I prefer the former* (the first one named). To say something is no longer true, use *used to* or *no longer*: *He used to be a teacher*, not *He is former*. Do not mix up *former* and *formal* (официальный).

senses.gloss: Having been a particular thing in the past, but not now.
examples: Two *former* presidents spoke at the funeral.
I ran into my *former* boss at the grocery store.
The museum is in a *former* train station.

senses.gloss: Belonging to an earlier time.
examples: After the fire, the old theater was restored to its *former* glory.
Since the illness he's been a shadow of his *former* self.
In *former* times, the river was the only road into the valley.

senses.gloss: First of two things just mentioned.
examples: Some students commute and some live on campus; the *former* group spends far less on rent.
You can pay now or in installments, but the *former* option saves you about $200.

position: attributive only — as an adjective it goes before the noun: *an outright lie*; after a verb *outright* is the adverb (*she refused outright*)
contrast: The adjective is stressed on the first syllable, OWT-ryt: *an outright ban*. The adverb, which follows the verb, is stressed on the second, owt-RYT: *refuse outright*, *buy a car outright* (for the full price at once), *killed outright* (instantly), *laugh outright* (openly). So *The ban is outright* is wrong; say *The ban is total* or *They banned it outright*.

senses.gloss: Complete and total, with no limits or exceptions.
examples: Several cities have passed an *outright* ban on fireworks.
The committee's answer was an *outright* rejection of the plan.

senses.gloss: Open and direct; not hidden or softened.
examples: That wasn't a mistake — it was an *outright* lie.
The meeting started politely and ended in *outright* hostility.

senses.gloss: Clear and unquestioned, with no need to share or count again.
examples: No candidate won an *outright* majority, so there will be a runoff.
She was the *outright* winner, ten points ahead of anyone else.

senses.gloss: Paid or given in full at once, with no conditions or installments.
examples: An *outright* purchase costs more up front than a lease.
Her grandparents gave her the house as an *outright* gift.

position: attributive only — after a verb use the adverb *indoors*: *The party is indoors*, not *The party is indoor*
contrast: *Indoor* goes before a noun (*an indoor pool*); *indoors* goes after a verb (*Let's eat indoors*, *The kids stayed indoors all day*). In everyday speech *inside* is more common than *indoors*: *Come inside, it's raining*. Russian *комнатная температура* is *room temperature*, not *indoor temperature*, which means the temperature inside a building.

senses.gloss: Built, located or done inside a building, not in the open air.
examples: The hotel has an *indoor* pool and a gym.
Our high school plays *indoor* soccer in the winter.
*Indoor* smoking is banned in bars across the state.

senses.gloss: Kept, used or suitable inside a home.
examples: *Indoor* cats usually live longer than cats that go outside.
Most *indoor* plants need less water in winter.
Kids, use your *indoor* voices, please.

position: attributive only — after a verb use the adverb *outdoors*: *The concert is outdoors*, not *The concert is outdoor*
contrast: *Outdoor* goes before a noun (*outdoor seating*); *outdoors* goes after a verb (*We ate outdoors*) and is also a noun in *the great outdoors* (природа, дикая природа). For a person who loves hiking and camping, Americans use the informal adjective *outdoorsy*, which can follow a verb: *She's very outdoorsy*, not *She's very outdoor*.

senses.gloss: Located, happening or used outside, not in a building.
examples: The restaurant added *outdoor* seating for the summer.
They held the wedding at an *outdoor* venue by the lake.
Put the *outdoor* furniture in the garage before the first frost.

senses.gloss: Connected with or fond of activities in nature, such as hiking and camping.
senses.ru: для активного отдыха, туристический; любящий природу
examples: He's never been the *outdoor* type.
The store sells *outdoor* gear like tents and hiking boots.

position: attributive only — after a verb use *alone*: *a lone rider*, but *The rider was alone*
contrast: Three words, three jobs. *Lone* goes before a noun and says there is only one: *a lone tree*. *Alone* goes after a verb: *She lives alone*. *Lonely* is the sad feeling (одинокий, тоскующий) and works in both positions: *a lonely old man*, *I felt lonely*. So *He was lone* is wrong. British *lone parent* is *single parent* in American English; *a lone wolf* is a person who prefers to act alone.

senses.gloss: Alone; with no other people or things nearby.
examples: A *lone* hiker was walking along the ridge.
There was a *lone* tree in the middle of the field.
The police believe a *lone* gunman fired the shots.

senses.gloss: Being the only one.
examples: She was the *lone* survivor of the crash.
The senator cast the *lone* vote against the bill.
Their *lone* goal came in the final minute.

position: attributive only — after a verb use *higher* or *on top*: *the upper shelf*, but *That shelf is higher*
comparison: not gradable — *upper* is itself an old comparative of *up*, so there is no *more upper* and no *upper than*; the related superlative is *uppermost*
contrast: Although *upper* looks like a comparative, it never takes *than*: *The attic is higher than the second floor*, not *upper than*. *Upper* names one of two or more levels: *the upper floors*, *the upper lip*. Idioms: *have the upper hand* (иметь преимущество), *keep a stiff upper lip* (не показывать чувств). The noun *upper* is the top part of a shoe, or slang for a stimulant drug.

senses.gloss: Higher in position; above another part.
examples: The *upper* floors of the building have the best views.
He has a small scar on his *upper* lip.
Most of this workout is for your *upper* body.

senses.gloss: Higher in rank, level or amount.
examples: The report went to *upper* management for approval.
Is there an *upper* age limit for the program?
The Senate is often called the *upper* house of Congress.

senses.gloss: Farther upstream, farther inland or farther north.
examples: Barges carry grain down from the *upper* Mississippi.
They moved from Brooklyn to *upper* Manhattan.

position: attributive only — after a verb use *inside*: *the inner door*, but *The door is inside*
comparison: not gradable — no *more inner*; the related superlative is *innermost*: *my innermost thoughts*
contrast: *Inner city* in American English is not the historic center (центр города): it means poorer, crowded neighborhoods near the center, as in *inner-city schools*. For the business center of a city, say *downtown*. After a verb *inner* does not work: use *inside* or rephrase. *Inner* feelings are private ones: *inner peace* = душевный покой.

senses.gloss: Inside; closer to the center of something.
examples: The *inner* walls of the house are made of drywall.
An infection of the *inner* ear can affect your balance.
Runners in the *inner* lane have the shortest distance to cover.

senses.gloss: Private and not shown to other people; of the mind or spirit.
examples: Meditation helped her find some *inner* peace.
He rarely talks about his *inner* life.
It took real *inner* strength to walk away.

senses.gloss: Closest to the center of power and trusted with its secrets.
examples: Only a few people in the governor's *inner* circle knew about the plan.
She was never part of the company's *inner* circle.

position: attributive only — after a verb use *outside* or *on the outside*: *the outer wall*, but *The wall is on the outside*
comparison: not gradable — no *more outer*; the related superlative is *outermost*: *the outermost planets*
contrast: *Outer* always needs a noun after it; after a verb use *outside* or *on the outside*. *Outer space* is космос. On medicine labels English says *external*, not *outer*: *For external use only* (для наружного применения).

senses.gloss: On the outside; farther from the center.
examples: Peel off the tough *outer* leaves of the cabbage.
The *outer* layer of the jacket is waterproof.
Comets come from the *outer* edges of the solar system.

senses.gloss: Farther from the center of a city or region.
examples: Rents are cheaper in the *outer* boroughs of New York.
We live in one of the *outer* suburbs, an hour from downtown.

senses.gloss: Seen from outside; showing on the surface rather than what someone really feels.
examples: Her *outer* calm hid how nervous she really was.
Don't judge people by their *outer* appearance.

position: attributive only — after a verb use *the only one*: *the sole witness*, but *She was the only one who saw it*
contrast: *Sole* is more formal than *only* and needs *the*, *a* or a possessive before it: *the sole reason*, *her sole goal*. The noun *sole* is the bottom of a shoe or foot (подошва, ступня) and a flatfish (морской язык), and *soul* (душа) sounds exactly the same. The adverb is *solely* (*solely responsible*). Legal phrases: *sole custody* (опека одного родителя), *sole proprietor* (индивидуальный предприниматель).

senses.gloss: Being the only one.
examples: His *sole* purpose in coming was to see his daughter.
The *sole* witness to the accident was a mail carrier.
Money was not the *sole* reason she took the job.

senses.gloss: Belonging to one person or group only; not shared.
examples: After the divorce, she was granted *sole* custody of the kids.
He is the *sole* owner of the business.
The company has *sole* rights to sell the drug in the U.S.

position: attributive only — as an adjective only before a noun: *a downright lie*; before another adjective it is the adverb (*downright rude*)
contrast: In American English *downright* is far more common as an adverb before an adjective: *downright rude*, *downright dangerous*, *It was downright cold*. As an adjective it goes only before a noun, usually a bad one: *a downright lie*, *downright nonsense*. *The lie was downright* is not English. The old sense 'blunt, frank' (*a downright man*) is now rare.

senses.gloss: Complete and total, used to stress something bad.
examples: What he told the jury was a *downright* lie.
Calling that car a bargain is *downright* nonsense.
The way they treated the new hire was a *downright* disgrace.

position: attributive only — after *the*, *an*, *this* or a possessive with a singular noun: *the entire day*; after a verb use *whole* or *intact*
contrast: Russian *весь* is often *all* in English, but the patterns differ: *all day* or *the entire day*, not *all the day* or *entire day*. With a singular noun *entire* needs *the*, *an*, *this* or a possessive: *the entire class*, *my entire life*, *an entire week*. With a plural it means 'whole groups of' and can stand alone: *Entire families lost their homes*. After a verb use *whole* or *intact*: *The vase was still whole*; *still entire* is formal and rare. The adverb is *entirely*.

senses.gloss: Whole; with no part left out.
examples: We spent the *entire* day at the beach.
I've lived in this town my *entire* life.
*Entire* neighborhoods were flooded after the storm.

senses.gloss: Complete in degree; total and without any doubt.
examples: The new baby has her *entire* attention these days.
After the injury, he put his *entire* focus on getting well.

position: attributive only — always after *the*, *this*, *that* or a possessive: *the very moment*, *her very words*
comparison: not gradable — the old superlative *veriest* is archaic
contrast: The everyday *very* is the adverb 'очень' (*very good*). The adjective *very* stands right before a noun, always after *the*, *this*, *that* or a possessive, and means 'exactly this' or 'the extreme': *the very day*, *the very top*. Russian *самый* is the trap: *самый конец* is *the very end*, but *самый красивый* is *the most beautiful*, never *the very beautiful*. In *the very best* and *the very first*, *very* is the adverb again, strengthening *best* or *first*. The adjective can never follow a verb.

senses.gloss: Exactly this one and no other.
examples: That's the *very* book I was looking for!
At that *very* moment, the lights went out.
They got married in the *very* church where they first met.

senses.gloss: At the extreme point of something: right at the beginning, end, top or bottom.
examples: Read the note at the *very* bottom of the page.
We stayed until the *very* end of the game.
The problem was clear from the *very* beginning.

senses.gloss: Just the thing itself, used to stress that it alone matters or has an effect.
examples: The *very* thought of public speaking makes me sweat.
Budget cuts threaten the *very* existence of the program.
The *very* idea of moving again made her tired.

position: both — but in the sense 'not dead' only before a noun (*a live lobster*, but *The lobster is still alive*); and in *real live* ('real, in person'); *live* follows a verb in the senses 'not recorded', 'carrying current' and 'working' (*The show is live*, *The wire is live*, *The site is live*)
contrast: The adjective rhymes with *five* (laɪv); the verb *live* rhymes with *give* (lɪv). In the sense 'not dead', *live* goes only before a noun; after a verb use *alive*: *They caught a live snake*, but *The snake was still alive*, not *still live*. *Living* works in both positions (*living things*, *Is he still living?*). *Live* is also an adverb after verbs of broadcasting and performing: *The game is shown live*, *She has never played live*. Do not confuse it with *lively* (оживлённый, энергичный): *a lively party* is fun and busy; *a live band* plays in front of you.

senses.gloss: Happening in front of an audience, or broadcast while it happens, not recorded.
examples: The bar has *live* music every Friday night.
All the major networks carried the debate as a *live* broadcast.
The show is *live*, so the hosts can't fix any mistakes.

senses.gloss: Living; not dead.
examples: You can pick out a *live* lobster from the tank.
The company says it does not test its products on *live* animals.
He fishes with *live* bait.

senses.gloss: Carrying electric current.
examples: Don't touch that cable — it could still be *live*.
The third rail is *live*, so stay off the subway tracks.

senses.gloss: Able to explode or fire; not a blank or a dud.
examples: The soldiers trained with *live* ammunition for the first time.
Construction workers dug up a *live* bomb from World War II.

senses.gloss: Working and available for people to use, of a website, app or system.
examples: The new website goes *live* on Monday.
The update is *live* for all users now.

senses.gloss: Still burning or glowing.
examples: Spread the *live* coals evenly under the grill.
Never dump *live* ashes into a trash can.

senses.gloss: Still being discussed and not yet settled; of current interest.
examples: Whether to build a new stadium is still a *live* issue in the city.
A four-day workweek remains a *live* possibility at the company.

senses.gloss: Real and in person, used in the informal phrase real live to show surprise or excitement.
examples: The kids were thrilled to meet a real *live* astronaut.
I'd never seen a real *live* movie star before.

position: attributive only — after a verb always *drunk*: *a drunken fan*, but *The fan was drunk*
form: the old past participle of *drink*, with -en
contrast: After a verb the word is *drunk*, never *drunken*: *He was drunk*, not *He was drunken*. Before a noun both occur, but they lean different ways: *drunk* is usual for people (*a drunk driver*; *drunk driving* is the everyday American term), while *drunken* is usual for actions and events (*a drunken brawl*, *a drunken rant*). *A drunk* is also a noun, a person who is often drunk (пьяница). The past participle of the verb is *drunk*: *I have drunk*, not *I have drunken*.

senses.gloss: Drunk, or often drunk, of a person.
examples: A *drunken* fan ran onto the field in the ninth inning.
The movie is about a *drunken* ex-cop trying to get sober.

senses.gloss: Caused by or showing the effects of too much alcohol.
examples: Police broke up a *drunken* fight outside the bar.
It was the *most drunken* party the fraternity had ever thrown.
He left a *drunken* voicemail he regretted the next morning.

position: attributive only — never after a verb: *the ship's maiden voyage*, not *the voyage was maiden*
form: from the old noun *maiden*, 'young unmarried woman'
contrast: *Maiden* as a noun (девушка, дева) is old-fashioned and poetic. The adjective lives on in fixed phrases: *maiden voyage*, *maiden flight*, *maiden speech* (the first of a kind) and *maiden name* (девичья фамилия). American forms often ask for *last name at birth* instead, and a man's earlier surname is never his *maiden name*. *A maiden aunt* (an older unmarried woman) sounds dated and can be unkind.

senses.gloss: First of its kind, used for a first trip, flight or speech.
examples: The Titanic sank on its *maiden* voyage in 1912.
The new rocket completed its *maiden* flight without a problem.
The senator gave her *maiden* speech on health care.

senses.gloss: Relating to a woman before she married.
examples: She kept her *maiden* name after the wedding.
Your mother's *maiden* name is a common security question at banks.

position: attributive only — never after a verb: *a mock trial*, not *the trial was mock*
contrast: The verb *mock* (насмехаться, передразнивать) is more common than the adjective: *The other kids mocked his accent*. The adjective always means 'not real'. A practice exam at school is *a mock exam* in British English but usually *a practice test* in American English; *mock trial* (a school competition that acts out a court case) and *mock election* are common in the US. A *mock-up* (noun) is a model of something that will be built.

senses.gloss: Done as practice, as an imitation of a real event.
examples: Our high school's *mock* trial team made it to the state finals.
The career center runs *mock* interviews for seniors.
The class held a *mock* election the week before the real one.

senses.gloss: Pretended, not sincere, usually as a joke.
examples: She threw up her hands in *mock* horror.
He raised an eyebrow in *mock* surprise when I showed up on time.

senses.gloss: Made to look like something else.
examples: He wore a black *mock* turtleneck under his blazer.
Her grandmother's *mock* apple pie uses crackers instead of apples.
